metadata.title: Miller v. French, 530 U.S. 327 (2000) (No. 99-224)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Miller v. French

Opinion filed: 2000-06-19

Docket No.: 99-224

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 326
• 120 S. Ct. 2246
• 530 U.S. 327
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 4296

Case holding summaries:
• ruling that "[p]rospective relief under a continuing, executory decree remains subject to alteration due to changes in the underlying law"
• discussing Hayburn’s Case, 2 U.S. (2 Dall) 408 (1792)
• "There is no logical inconsistency in saying both (1) a motion (to terminate) "shall operate as a stay," and (2
• "[W]here Congress has made its intent clear, `[courts] must give effect to that intent.'"
• discussing the difference between "shall" and "may" in statutory interpretation
• inmate class action initially brought against Indiana prison officials, including superintendent of correctional facility
• ‚*W+e should not construe a statute to displace courts’ traditional equitable authority absent the ‘clearest command’ or an ‘inescapable inference’ to the contrary*.+‛
• characterizing Klein’s holding as limited to pending cases
• referring to the "mandatory term `shall'"
• "While the boundaries between the three branches are not `hermetically' sealed, the Constitution prohibits one branch from encroaching on the central prerogatives of another."
• warning that courts should be chary about interpreting statutes to restrict the scope of traditional judicial review absent the "clearest command" or an "inescapable inference to the contrary" (citations and internal quotation marks omitted)
• “[W]e should not construe a statute to displace courts’ traditional equitable authority absent the clearest command, or an inescapable inference to the contrary.”
• prospective relief may change as statutory foundation changes
• ruling that “[p]rospective relief under a continuing, executory decree remains subject to alteration due to changes in the underlying law”
• rejecting a "saving" interpretation of automatic stay provisions because it "would subvert the plain meaning of the statute"
• counseling courts to avoid "constitutionally doubtful constructions"
• "By establishing new standards for the enforcement of prospective relief, . . . Congress has altered the relevant underlying law."
• The Constitution enumerates and separates the power of the three branches of Government in Articles I, II, and III, and it is this 'very structure of the Constitution that exemplifies the concept of separation of powers."
• explaining that separation of powers doctrine “prohibits one branch from encroaching on the central prerogatives of another”
• noting motion "for a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction to enjoin the operation of the automatic stay"
